Analysis:
Both hypotheses address dual-intervention strategies in hepatocellular carcinoma by combining metabolic modulation with immune microenvironment targeting. Hypothesis 1 combines inhibition of methionine adenosyltransferase (aiming to reduce SAM/MTA‐driven T cell exhaustion) with blockade of the CXCL11/CXCR3 axis to prevent recruitment of T cells that support cancer stem cell renewal. Its novelty lies in merging metabolic correction with a chemokine axis that may be influencing the tumor stem cell compartment. Although reviewers noted the need for deeper mechanistic explanations and more rigorous preclinical evidence, its components are relatively defined and offer specific molecular markers (e.g. SAM/MTA levels and exhaustion markers) to assess efficacy, making it fairly testable. The specificity of the chemokine axis, despite concerns about dual roles in tumor immunity, suggests a targetable pathway that may be managed with proper experimental design. In contrast, Hypothesis 2 couples the inhibition of dysregulated methionine metabolism with blockade of the C5a receptor in tumor-associated macrophages to reverse T cell exhaustion. While the involvement of macrophages and complement signaling provides an innovative angle, the review raised more concerns regarding the integration of the mechanisms, possible compensatory immunosuppressive pathways, and systemic off-target effects given the broad role of complement in innate immunity. Overall, Hypothesis 1 stands out for its clearer mechanistic components and potentially safer, more controlled modulation of the immune response, even though both proposals require further empirical validation.
